content: Ammonium lactate is a topical medication approved by the FDA for the treatment of dry, scaly skin conditions such as xerosis and ichthyosis vulgaris. It is also used for temporary relief of itching associated with these conditions. Common side effects include burning sensations, erythema (redness of the skin), skin peeling, and stinging. For adults, the recommended usage involves shaking the product well, applying it to the affected areas, and rubbing it in thoroughly. It should be used twice daily or as directed by a physician. There is limited information regarding off-label uses of ammonium lactate in adults. In pediatric patients, there is limited information on FDA-labeled indications and dosages. However, safety and effectiveness have been demonstrated in infants and children, with no unusual toxic effects reported. Off-label uses in pediatric patients are also not well-documented. Ammonium lactate cream is contraindicated in patients with a known hypersensitivity to any of its ingredients. Sun exposure to treated areas should be minimized or avoided, and the medication should be discontinued if hypersensitivity reactions occur. Adverse reactions reported during clinical trials include transient stinging, burning, erythema, and peeling, with varying frequencies. Patients with ichthyosis may experience a higher incidence of these reactions. Less common adverse effects include irritation, eczema, petechiae, dryness, and hyperpigmentation. There is limited information on drug interactions, pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of ammonium lactate. Animal studies at doses up to five times the human dose have shown no evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the fetus, but there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Therefore, ammonium lactate should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. Its effects on lactation and excretion in human milk are not well understood, so caution is advised when administering it to nursing mothers. Clinical studies in geriatric populations did not include sufficient numbers of subjects aged 65 and older to determine whether they respond differently from younger patients. Dose selection for elderly patients should be cautious. There is no specific FDA guidance on its use in relation to gender, race, renal impairment, hepatic impairment, or immunocompromised patients. Ammonium lactate is administered topically, and there is limited information on monitoring, IV compatibility, and overdose management. In case of suspected overdose, the National Poison Help hotline should be contacted immediately. There is no established interaction between ammonium lactate and alcohol, but patients should consult their doctor regarding potential effects. The medication is marketed under the brand name AMMONIUM LACTATE®. There is limited information on look-alike drug names, storage, and patient counseling in the drug label.
